Building the runtime that turns any app into a platform. Mobile Architecture Super Apps Product Strategy Modular Design Digital Transformation How Much of Your Existing App Should Become Modular? FinClip 7 min read · Just now -- Listen Share Modular delivery can solve a real mobile problem. A regional service no longer has to wait behind a core payment release. A campaign can change while its commercial window is still open. A product team can improve a bounded journey without coordinating every detail with the main app roadmap. Once those benefits become visible, the idea can expand too far. The programme begins to measure progress by the number of modules created. Existing screens are separated because the technology allows it. Teams start treating “native” as legacy and “modular” as the destination for the entire app. That target overlooks an important feature of established mobile products: different parts of the app have different customer, technical and operating consequences. Some capabilities belong close to the host. Some gain meaningful independence when modularised. Others should remain on the web or in a separate product. The design task is to find those boundaries deliberately. Press enter or click to view image in full size Modularity is a spectrum The word “module” can describe several different arrangements. An engineering team may divide one native codebase into internal build modules. A platform may load a feature conditionally. A Super App may run separately delivered mini apps inside a controlled runtime. A service may remain external while the host provides a connected handoff. These models should not be treated as interchangeable. They do share several boundary questions: what belongs together, what can change independently, which interfaces must remain stable and who owns the result. Google’s current guide to Android app modularisation defines modularisation as organising a codebase into loosely coupled, self-contained parts with clear purposes. It also warns that overly fine-grained modules introduce build complexity and boilerplate, while excessively coarse modules lose many of the benefits. That guidance concerns Gradle and Android code architecture, rather than dynamically delivered mini apps. The principle still travels well: a boundary creates value when it increases useful independence. Every boundary also adds an interface and operating cost. A three-zone mobile portfolio For planning purposes, an existing app can be viewed through three delivery zones. Zone 1: the core native product This zone contains capabilities closely tied to the app’s primary promise and trust relationship. Examples may include authentication, account security, payment authorisation, transaction confirmation, core navigation and heavily used product journeys. The reasons to keep a capability here are operational as much as technical: It reaches most customers. Failure has a high financial, regulatory or reputational consequence. It depends deeply on native state or device behaviour. It must change with other core capabilities. One team needs complete visibility during an incident. The benefit of an independent release is relatively small. The native core can still be cleanly structured internally. Keeping a capability native does not require accepting a tangled monolith. Zone 2: bounded modular services This zone contains coherent customer tasks that benefit from the host relationship while needing a different delivery rhythm. An appointment service may use basic identity and appear under Support. A regional product journey may serve only one market. A loyalty campaign may need several changes during a quarter. A calculator or document-submission service may have a dedicated business owner and a limited set of host dependencies. These are potential candidates for a controlled runtime because they can be developed, released, monitored and withdrawn within a clear boundary. Google’s page on common modularisation patterns recommends low coupling and high cohesion: parts should be as independent as practical, and the elements inside each module should belong to a closely related domain. Again, the page addresses Android project modules. Its vocabulary is useful when assessing customer-facing modules as well. A service that needs detailed knowledge of several neighbours, shares their release schedule and cannot be diagnosed separately may not have found a real boundary yet. Zone 3: web or independent services Some services need only a clear handoff from the main app. They may have a separate audience or brand, an independent legal relationship, a specialist operating model or very low usage among the host’s customers. Deep integration can make responsibility less clear or add permanent navigation for a task few people need. A secure mobile website may suit a low-frequency, self-contained journey. A separate app may suit a frequent product with its own customer acquisition and engagement model.
